extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether a source is reliable for supporting particular statements in English Wikipedia articles, covering types of sources, contextual factors, and special cases (medicine, BLPs, breaking news, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Source must be credible for the particular claims supported
rubrics_metrics.description: Each book, article, or other source needs to be credible for supporting the particular claim(s) it supports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper sourcing always depends on context; editors must be able to explain why they relied on that source. No source is 'always reliable' or 'always unreliable' for everything. Evaluate whether the source directly supports the information as presented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer reliable, independent, published sources with reputation for fact-checking
rubrics_metrics.description: Articles should be based on reliable, independent, published sources with a reputation for fact-checking and accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This includes scholarly publications, reputable news outlets, and other publications with editorial oversight. The qualifications (publisher, author expertise) should be demonstrable to others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context matters when judging reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: The reliability of a source depends on context; each source must be carefully weighed to judge whether it is reliable for the statement being made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Information provided in passing by an otherwise reliable source may not be reliable for a specific claim; prefer sources focused on the topic at hand. Consider whether the source directly supports the specific fact or interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age matters — prefer current sources in many fields
rubrics_metrics.description: Older sources may be inaccurate because new information has been brought to light; newer sources are generally preferred in medicine and rapidly changing fields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check that older sources have not been superseded. Sometimes sources are too new (e.g., breaking news, preliminary primary reports), in which case waiting for verification may be appropriate; guard against recentism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usage by other sources as a signal of reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: How accepted and high-quality reliable sources use a given source provides evidence for its reliability and reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Widespread, consistent citation without comment supports reputation. If outside citation is main indicator, take care to adhere to other guidelines and avoid unduly representing contentious claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer secondary sources; use primary sources with caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Articles should rely on secondary sources whenever possible; primary sources are often difficult to use appropriately and must be used with caution to avoid original research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secondary sources like reviews, monographs, and textbooks are often preferable. Interpretive claims about primary sources must be supported by secondary sources. Use templates to flag primary-source concerns when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliable scholarship: peer review and reputable academic presses
rubrics_metrics.description: Material vetted by the scholarly community (peer-reviewed journals, scholarly monographs, reputable academic presses) is regarded as reliable when published by reputable venues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware some scholarly material may be outdated, controversial, or ignored; try to cite current scholarly consensus when available. Evaluate journal reputation and editorial board when in doubt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch for predatory journals and sham peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Predatory journals have token or no meaningful peer review and publish for fees; such journals are of very low quality and should be treated similarly to self-published sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check editorial board, inclusion in appropriate citation indexes, and independent evidence of review. Treat material from predatory journals with caution and generally avoid it for substantive claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preprints and repositories are generally unreliable (especially for medicine)
rubrics_metrics.description: Preprints and other non-peer-reviewed self-published materials (arXiv, medRxiv, bioRxiv, Zenodo) are seldom reliable sources and are not permitted for medical content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They may sometimes meet criteria for acceptable self-published sources or be used as open-access links for subsequently published work, but exercise extreme caution.

rubrics_metrics.name: News organizations: well-established outlets generally reliable for facts
rubrics_metrics.description: News reporting from well-established news outlets is generally considered reliable for statements of fact, though errors can occur—less-established outlets are generally less reliable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wire services should be cited with the agency and newspapers often reprint agency copy; scholarly sources are preferable for academic topics. Signals of reliability include corrections and COI disclosures. Evaluate on a case-by-case basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial/opinion pieces are reliable for attributed opinions but rarely for facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial commentary, analysis and opinion pieces are reliable primary sources for statements attributed to the author, but are rarely reliable for statements of fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using opinion content, identify the author and attribute opinions in-text rather than representing them as factual statements. Specialists' opinions may be more reliable for certain viewpoints.

rubrics_metrics.name: News aggregators: judge reliability based on the original source
rubrics_metrics.description: Websites that aggregate or reprint items from other sources may be a curated feed; reliability should be judged based on the original source and prefer direct links to the original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aggregators (e.g., MSN, Yahoo News) are not substitutes for original reporting; avoid citing the aggregator when the original source is available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vendor/e-commerce sources are limited and usually unsuitable for analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Vendor pages and e-commerce sites primarily exist to sell products and are generally not appropriate as secondary sources, though they may be used to verify bibliographic details like titles and running times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using vendor-provided rankings when unstable or self-published; replace with journalistic or academic sources if possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biased or partisan sources may be reliable in context but require caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Reliable sources are not required to be neutral; biased sources may be reliable for the views they express but are rarely reliable for neutral factual claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider editorial control, reputation for fact-checking, and independence. Attribute viewpoints in-text and be cautious about using partisan sources for factual assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Questionable sources are generally unsuitable for contentious claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Questionable sources—those with poor fact-checking, lack of editorial oversight, or apparent conflicts of interest—are generally unsuitable for citing contentious claims about third parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these sources only rarely and with clear limitations; beware websites that 'sound reliable' but lack reputation. Examples include content farms and promotional sites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sponsored content should be treated as non-independent/self-published
rubrics_metrics.description: Sponsored content (paid articles formatted like normal content) is non-independent and should be treated as self-published and primary in nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reliable publications clearly indicate sponsored content; treat undisclosed sponsored content as questionable. Sponsored supplements to journals often lack independent peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symposia and journal supplements often problematic
rubrics_metrics.description: Symposia and supplements may be sponsored by industry and lack independent editorial oversight and peer review, making them often unacceptable sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not all supplements are unacceptable; check for sponsorship, editorial policy, and independence. Look for signs like 'Suppl.' in citations and investigate funding and review procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-published sources largely unacceptable; limited exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-published books, personal websites, blogs, tweets, and forum posts are generally not acceptable; exceptions exist for established experts and for subjects about themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Never use self-published sources as third-party sources about living people. If an established expert has relevant, previously vetted work, their self-published material may sometimes be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: User-generated content is generally unacceptable as a source
rubrics_metrics.description: Websites whose content is largely user-generated (social media, forums, most wikis, video/image hosting) are generally unacceptable as sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions may exist for verified official accounts or for certain content about themselves, but ratings, user reviews, and user-generated entries should be treated with caution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-published/questionable sources may be used about themselves under strict conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-published or questionable sources may be used as sources of information about themselves provided the material is not unduly self-serving, does not make exceptional claims about third parties, is authentic, and the article is not based primarily on such sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The same requirements apply to social networking pages; use such material minimally and prefer independent sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources produced by machine learning (LLMs) are generally unreliable
rubrics_metrics.description: Generative AI outputs (LLMs, ChatGPT) are generally unreliable, prone to hallucination, and akin to self-published/user-generated content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: LLM-produced content may include false information and fabricated citations; treat it as unreliable and avoid using it as a source. See specific notes on LLMs and examples of hallucinated citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special care for Biographies of Living Persons (BLP)
rubrics_metrics.description: Contentious material about living persons that is unsourced or poorly sourced—whether negative, positive, or neutral—must be removed immediately and without waiting for discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the strictest sourcing standards in any namespace when dealing with living persons. Never rely on self-published sources for material about living persons except in tightly constrained, verifiable circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary, secondary, tertiary sources explained
rubrics_metrics.description: Wikipedia prefers reliable secondary sources; tertiary sources (textbooks, almanacs) may be cited; primary sources require caution to avoid original research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primary sources can be used for specific facts but interpretive claims require secondary sources. Avoid large blocks of material based purely on primary sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medical claims require high-quality secondary sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideal biomedical sources include general/systematic reviews, reputable medical journals, standard textbooks, and guidelines from reputable expert bodies; preprints and self-published sources are not permitted for medical content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Medical info must reflect current medical knowledge; prefer secondary sources and verify accuracy. Use special medical sourcing guidance and templates where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fringe theories: parity of sources and avoiding undue weight
rubrics_metrics.description: Fringe theories should not be given equal weight; include fringe material only if supported by reliable, verifiable sources, and balance by citing reliable criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In fringe-topic articles, some non-peer-reviewed sources may be used to describe the fringe view, but overall coverage must rely on reliable sources and not give undue weight to fringe claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotations: accuracy and sourcing paramount
rubrics_metrics.description: The accuracy of quoted material is paramount; best practice is to take quoted text from the original source cited, especially for living persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If quoting from a secondary source, ensure it cites the original. Attribute and do not interpret quoted material without a reliable secondary source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Academic consensus claims require direct sourcing
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements that a consensus exists (e.g., 'There is an academic consensus that...') require reliable sourcing that directly states that consensus, not editor inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use methodologically sound surveys or review articles that explicitly discuss the extent of agreement; avoid novel synthesis of disparate material to assert consensus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statements of opinion: attribute clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: Some sources are reliable for statements about their author's opinions but not for factual assertions; attribute opinions to the author in the article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Never use self-published sources as sources for material about living people unless written by the subject. For opinions, clarify they are opinions and identify the author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breaking news: exercise caution and prefer later verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Breaking-news reports often contain serious inaccuracies; it's better to wait a day or two for verification rather than adding unverified details to articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek multiple independent sources, verified eyewitness reports, and be wary of anonymous or unconfirmed reports. All breaking news stories are primary sources and must be treated cautiously; use 'current' templates where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headlines and subheadlines are not reliable sources by themselves
rubrics_metrics.description: News headlines are written to attract attention and may be overstated or lack context; if information is supported by the body, cite the body rather than the headline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using headlines as the source of a claim; verify in the full text of the article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deprecated and blacklisted sources should not be used
rubrics_metrics.description: Some sources are deprecated or blacklisted on Wikipedia due to fabrication or other serious accuracy issues and should not be used except in narrow exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deprecation is decided via community discussion; deprecated sources should not be used to support factual claims and may only be used rarely for commentary on the source itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid circular sourcing and churnalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Be cautious of circular sourcing where Wikipedia is used as a source by news sites or where news outlets merely reprint press releases (churnalism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer original investigative sources and independent verification; treat press releases as self-published and avoid using outlets that simply republish others' content without independent reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signals of reliability in news organizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicators that a news organization engages in fact-checking and has a reputation for accuracy include publication of corrections and disclosure of conflicts of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these signals when evaluating news outlets, but still judge stories case-by-case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wire-service duplication: multiple outlets reprinting the same wire equals one source
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple sources should not be asserted for any single wire-service article since reprints are essentially the same source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite the original wire service where possible rather than multiple reprints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leaks and anonymous reports should be treated cautiously
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless reported by a reliable source, leaks and anonymous reports should not normally be used or cited directly in articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wait for confirmation from reliable, independent reporting before including information based on leaks.
